title: Control of giant sensitive plant in perennial crop fields - Vietnam

Header: Control of giant sensitive plant in perennial crop fields - Vietnam

Prevention: Clean tools and farm machinery after working in infested areas to prevent seeds being spread.
Do not accept potentially contaminated materials, e.g. fill dirt, hay or soil.
Control established populations near waterways to prevent spread during flooding and storm events.
Avoid seeding to prevent the buildup of a seed bank.
Monitoring: Additional relevant crops: perennial crops such as citrus, litchi, longan, and mango.
Scrambling, strongly branched shrub, forming dense thickets.
Stems, 4–5, angled in cross-section, covered with sharp, recurved spines.
Leaves bright- green, twice-divided (10–20cm long), with 4–9 pairs of leaflet branchlets.
Flowers pinkish-violet, round heads (12mm across), borne singly or in small groups on hairy stalks.
Pods flat, softly spiny on edges, elongated (8–35 mm long and 3–10 mm wide); break into one-seeded joints.
Check pastures and crop fields every two to four weeks, consider direct control if present.
Check monthly for presence of the weed in wetlands and along waterways.
Water and storm events can spread seeds.
Direct Control: Wearing gloves, hand pull or hoe, or till the land twice per year, when weed is young/easier to remove.
Remove roots at least 15cm below surface to prevent regrowth.
Cut branches regularly, before seeding, then collect and burn, alongside other control methods.
900g a.i/ha) mixtures can be used in seedbeds.

Restrictions: Use of chemical herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistance.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, and pre-harvest interval.
The use of pre-emergence herbicides refers to the emergence of the weed.
U (unlikely to present acute hazard in normal use), WSSA resistance group 2.
Spraying should be carried out when the weed is actively growing.
Thorough wetting of the foliage is necessary.
These foliar herbicides will also affect other pasture legumes.
The best approach to control the weed is usually to combine different methods.
Control may include chemical, mechanical, fire and biological methods combined with land management changes and will be site-specific.
